name: RetentionPolicy
purpose: Declarative binding of a data class to a maximum lifetime, enforced by scheduled purge and blocked at write-time if unclassified.
api_signature:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import timedelta
from typing import Protocol

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetentionPolicy:
    data_class: str
    max_age: timedelta
    legal_basis: str
    deletion_mode: str  # 'hard' | 'crypto_shred' | 'anonymize'

class RetentionEnforcer(Protocol):
    def bind(self, policy: RetentionPolicy) -> None: ...
    def enforce_on_write(self, data_class: str, record_id: str) -> None: ...
    def sweep(self) -> int: ...
invariants: Every persisted record MUST be tagged with a data_class that maps to a registered RetentionPolicy; writes of untagged data SHALL be rejected.
max_age MUST be finite and > 0; an open-ended 'keep forever' policy CANNOT be registered without an explicit legal_basis override.
deletion_mode MUST be one of 'hard', 'crypto_shred', or 'anonymize'; other values SHALL raise on bind.
The sweep job MUST be idempotent and SHALL not delete records under an active LegalHold.
Every purge action MUST emit an entry to the TamperEvidentAuditLog with the policy id and record count.
extension_contract: Target applications register a policy per data_class and plug in deletion adapters (SQL delete, object-store lifecycle, crypto-shred key destroy). Custom deletion_modes are added by implementing a DeletionAdapter and binding it through the registry.
consumption_example:
from datetime import timedelta

policy = RetentionPolicy(
    data_class='access_token',
    max_age=timedelta(days=90),
    legal_basis='GDPR Art 5(1)(e) storage limitation',
    deletion_mode='hard',
)
enforcer.bind(policy)
purged = enforcer.sweep()

sources.locator: Requirement 3.2 — do not store cardholder data beyond retention need

why_essential: Retention without a shared primitive decays into per-table ad-hoc cron jobs that drift from policy; a single binding fixes data-class-to-lifetime across the whole target.
alternatives_considered: Database TTL indexes — only work per collection and ignore legal_basis, legal hold, and deletion_mode.
Cron scripts per table — drift silently when schema evolves and produce no audit evidence.
Leaving retention to ops runbooks — moves the rule outside code review and fails SOC 2 evidence.
